abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a novel information-theoretic framework for distributed learning systems that fundamentally reconceptualizes how computation and communication are jointly optimized across networked computing nodes. Unlike traditional approaches that treat communication compression and model accuracy as competing objectives, we introduce a unified optimization landscape based on conditional entropy bounds and rate-distortion theory. Our analysis reveals that existing distributed learning paradigms operate within a suboptimal region of the information bottleneck plane, and we prove that a new class of structured compression codes can achieve the theoretical minimum communication complexity while maintaining near-centralized model performance. The key innovation lies in our derivation of achievable regions for distributed stochastic gradient descent under arbitrary network topologies, which establishes that computational compression and gradient sparsification can be synergistically combined through a novel lattice-based encoding scheme. We further demonstrate that this framework naturally accommodates heterogeneous data distributions and dynamic network conditions without requiring synchronization barriers. Experiments on communication-constrained edge computing scenarios validate our theoretical findings, showing that the proposed paradigm reduces communication overhead by orders of magnitude compared to baselines while maintaining statistical utility. This work opens a new theoretical direction for designing communication-efficient distributed systems and provides foundational principles for next-generation federated learning architectures.

We present a significantly enhanced theoretical analysis of graph neural network expressive power that addresses critical gaps in the Weisfeiler-Lehman hierarchy framework. While prior work established that message-passing neural networks are bounded by the 1-WL test, the precise relationship between subgraph structure encoding and discrimination capability remains underexplored. We introduce the concept of k-order subgraph isomorphism invariants and prove that incorporating these structural features enables GNNs to distinguish a strictly larger class of non-isomorphic graphs than standard color refinement. Our main theoretical contribution is the derivation of tight upper bounds on the discriminative power achievable by permutation-invariant graph encoders under message-passing constraints, which reveal that existing theoretical characterizations underestimate the expressive limitations of local aggregation operations. We further establish connections between our framework and spectral graph theory, demonstrating that eigenvector-based methods exhibit complementary discrimination capabilities to message-passing approaches. The analysis yields a principled approach for designing aggregation functions that explicitly encode higher-order structural information, leading to improved theoretical guarantees on graph isomorphism testing. Extensive experiments on synthetic graph datasets validate our theoretical predictions, showing that the proposed architectural modifications substantially improve performance on tasks requiring fine-grained structural discrimination while maintaining polynomial-time computability.

This paper introduces EdgeFlow, a revolutionary edge computing architecture designed for real-time intelligent data processing at the network periphery. Unlike conventional cloud-centric approaches that suffer from latency bottlenecks and bandwidth constraints, EdgeFlow implements a hierarchical federated intelligence framework where edge devices collaboratively perform distributed inference while preserving data locality. The system architecture comprises three novel components: a lightweight model compression engine that enables deep neural network deployment on resource-constrained edge devices, a probabilistic task offloading mechanism based on multi-agent reinforcement learning, and an adaptive model synchronization protocol that minimizes communication overhead through selective gradient compression. EdgeFlow introduces a paradigm shift by treating edge devices not merely as data collectors but as intelligent computing nodes capable of autonomous decision-making and peer-to-peer collaboration. The system dynamically provisions computational resources based on workload characteristics and device capabilities, achieving a balance between inference latency, energy consumption, and prediction accuracy. We deploy EdgeFlow across a network of 500 heterogeneous edge devices in a smart city infrastructure, demonstrating its ability to process over one million events per second with sub-10-millisecond response times. Compared to traditional edge-cloud architectures, EdgeFlow reduces bandwidth consumption by 65% and improves system reliability under dynamic network conditions by 80%.

We present CloudDB-Optimizer, a significantly enhanced query processing system that addresses the critical challenge of adaptive optimization in cloud-native database environments. Traditional query optimizers rely on static statistics and rule-based heuristics that fail to capture the dynamic nature of modern workloads and data distributions in cloud settings. CloudDB-Optimizer introduces a novel online learning architecture that continuously adapts query execution strategies based on real-time workload patterns and runtime feedback. The system integrates three key innovations: a lightweight neural cost model that predicts query execution characteristics with sub-millisecond latency, an incremental plan space exploration algorithm that balances optimization time with plan quality, and a learned cardinality estimation module that handles correlated attributes and skewed distributions more accurately than classical histogram-based approaches. We design the system with a modular architecture that enables seamless integration with existing cloud database engines through a standard optimizer interface. Extensive evaluation on production workloads from a major e-commerce platform demonstrates that CloudDB-Optimizer reduces average query response time by 38% for complex analytical queries and achieves a 52% improvement for multi-way join operations. The system exhibits robust adaptation to workload shifts and data skew, maintaining consistent performance improvements across diverse query patterns without requiring manual tuning or statistics refresh.
